summary: Describes version 2.1 of the Handle System protocol, which client software uses for both handle resolution and administration. It covers how a client locates the responsible handle server for any handle and defines the messages exchanged between client and server. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the conversation script for the Handle System. It tells a program how to find the right helper and exactly what to say to look up or change a permanent name.

subtitle: The wire protocol clients use to talk to Handle System servers.

tldr.problem: Handle System clients and servers need a standard protocol specification so any implementation can communicate with any other implementation. The protocol must handle handle resolution, administration, authentication, distributed services, and security features like digital signatures.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3652 defines a request-response protocol where clients send messages containing an envelope (for delivery), header (for operation codes and options), body (operation-specific data), and optional credential (for signatures or authentication codes). The protocol supports both UDP (with message fragmentation) and TCP, handles service referrals for distributed architecture, and includes a challenge-response authentication mechanism.
tldr.outcome: Vendors can implement Handle System clients and servers that all interoperate using a single standard protocol. The specification has been stable enough to support decades of implementations.

today: RFC 3652 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. Protocol version 2.1 specified here remains the current standard. The Handle System website documents any later developments or extensions to the protocol.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
RFC 3652 specifies version 2.1 of the Handle System protocol, a client-server protocol for accessing handles. Clients use it to look up handle values (resolution) and to add, delete, or modify handles and values (administration). The protocol is independent of the service architecture or data model details specified in RFC 3651, and implementations can support earlier protocol versions alongside version 2.1. The protocol works over both UDP (User Datagram Protocol) for request-response transactions and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) for longer interactions or when large messages require multiple packets.

Key features of the protocol include support for service referrals (a server telling a client to ask a different server), client authentication using public-key or secret-key cryptography, server authentication through digital signatures, data encryption using session keys, and message fragmentation for UDP packet size limits. The protocol uses the standard network byte order (Big-Endian) for multi-byte values and UTF-8 encoding for all text, ensuring compatibility across different platforms and languages.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the language clients and servers speak. It defines what a question looks like, what an answer looks like, and how they know they're talking to the real server.

sections.title: Message Structure
sections.content:
Every message exchanged under the protocol has four sections. The Message Envelope is always present and has a fixed size of 20 bytes. It contains the protocol version (currently 2.1), flags for compression and encryption, a session ID, a request ID (for matching responses to requests), a sequence number (for reassembling fragmented messages), and the message length. The Message Envelope is never protected by signatures because it is needed to deliver and reassemble the message.

The Message Header is also always present and has a fixed 24-byte size. It contains an operation code specifying what the client wants (resolve, add, delete, authenticate, establish a session, etc.), a response code indicating success or what error occurred, operation flags for options like requesting a digital signature, the serial number of service information the client is using, recursion count, expiration time, and the size of the message body. The Message Body is operation-specific; it may be empty, and its format depends on which operation code and response code are in the Message Header. The Message Credential (optional) carries digital signatures or message authentication codes to prove the message came from who it claims to and has not been modified.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is like a letter with an envelope (to deliver it), a header (saying what you want), a body (with the details), and optionally a signature to prove it's real.

sections.title: Protocol Operations
sections.content:
The protocol defines many operation types, each with specific request and response formats. Query operations retrieve handle values by sending the handle name and optionally a list of specific indexes or data types to retrieve. The server responds with the matching values (or an error if the handle doesn't exist). Administrative operations add, delete, or modify handle values or entire handles, and these require client authentication. Session operations establish, maintain, and terminate communication sessions that persist across multiple requests, allowing authentication information and TCP connections to be reused.

Each operation can include various option flags such as the Authoritative flag (asking for the primary server), the Certified flag (requesting a digital signature), the Recursive flag (asking the server to forward the request if needed), and the Keep Connection flag (asking the server not to close the TCP connection). The protocol supports service referrals, where a server tells a client that the handle is managed by a different service and provides the address and credentials of that service. Named authority delegation also uses referrals to direct clients to Local Handle Services managing child naming authorities. The recursion count prevents infinite loops of forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: Different operations let you look up handles, change them, prove who you are, and manage long conversations with a server.

sections.title: Client Authentication and Signatures
sections.content:
For operations that modify handles or access restricted data, the server challenges the client to prove its identity. The Handle System uses a challenge-response authentication protocol that works with both public-key and secret-key cryptography. The server sends a challenge (usually a random number), and the client computes a response by encrypting or signing the challenge with its secret key. The server verifies the response by decrypting it or checking the signature against the client's public key. This exchange happens within a session established for that purpose, protecting the credentials from exposure.

The protocol also supports server authentication through digital signatures. When a client requests the Certified flag, the server signs its response using its private key. The client can then verify the signature using the server's public key, which is provided in the service information (the HS_SITE value). The signature proves both that the response came from the legitimate server and that it has not been tampered with. The protocol also supports Message Authentication Codes (MACs) computed using a session key established between client and server, providing both authentication and integrity checking for encrypted sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: To prove you're allowed to make changes, you answer a challenge with your secret key. To verify a server is real, you check its digital signature using its public key.

sections.title: Transmission and Message Handling
sections.content:
The protocol supports both UDP and TCP. UDP is simpler but has a 512-byte packet size limit, so large messages must be fragmented. Each fragment gets its own Message Envelope with the truncated flag set and a sequence number so the receiver can reassemble them in order. The specification recommends retransmitting after 2-5 seconds if no response is received, trying other servers or service interfaces first before retrying the same server. TCP allows larger messages and stream-based transmission. A message's total size is limited by a 4-byte unsigned integer, but messages can be fragmented into multiple messages if needed.

The Message Envelope size information must be accurate so the receiver knows how much data to reassemble. The protocol includes flags for compression (using the same method as FTP) and encryption (using a pre-established session key). The specification recommends that servers support multiple concurrent connections, not block on receiving TCP data, and close connections after responding unless the client requests the Keep Connection flag to reuse the connection for multiple operations.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages can be broken into pieces for UDP, reassembled at the other end, or sent as streams over TCP. Big messages are split up, then put back together from the sequence numbers.
